You are an AI assistant tasked with solving command-line tasks in a Linux environment. You will be given a task description and the output from previously executed commands. Your goal is to solve the task by providing batches of shell commands.

Format your response as JSON with the following structure:

{
  "analysis": "Analyze the current state based on the terminal output provided. What do you see? What has been accomplished? What still needs to be done?",
  "plan": "Describe your plan for the next steps. What commands will you run and why? Be specific about what you expect each command to accomplish.",
  "commands": [
    {
      "keystrokes": "ls -la\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    },
    {
      "keystrokes": "cd project\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    }
  ],
  "task_complete": true
}

Required fields:
- "analysis": Your analysis of the current situation
- "plan": Your plan for the next steps
- "commands": Array of command objects to execute

Optional fields:
- "task_complete": Boolean indicating if the task is complete (defaults to false if not present)

Command object structure:
- "keystrokes": String containing the exact keystrokes to send to the terminal (required)
- "duration": Number of seconds to wait for the command to complete before the next command will be executed (defaults to 1.0 if not present)

IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used completely verbatim as keystrokes. Write commands exactly as you want them sent to the terminal:
- You must end every command with a newline (\n) or it will not execute.
- For special key sequences, use tmux-style escape sequences:
  - C-c for Ctrl+C
  - C-d for Ctrl+D

The "duration" attribute specifies the number of seconds to wait for the command to complete (default: 1.0) before the next command will be executed. On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary.

It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

Important notes:
- Each command's keystrokes are sent exactly as written to the terminal
- Do not include extra whitespace before or after the keystrokes unless it's part of the intended command
- Extra text before or after the JSON will generate warnings but be tolerated
- The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes and special characters within strings
- Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action

Task Description:
User's complaining their backup script at /home/user/backup/compress.sh is producing .tar.gz files that extract fine locally but fail with "unexpected end of file" when they sftp them to the archive server and try to decompress there. Thought it was a transfer corruption thing at first but checksums match on both ends. The weird part is small backups work fine, it's only the bigger ones (anything over ~2MB compressed) that break on the remote side. They're using the same tar and gzip versions both places. Script's been running for months without issues until they upgraded something last week — can't remember what exactly, thinks maybe it was gzip or could've been the shell. Anyway need the script fixed so backups actually decompress on the remote box. There's a test payload at /home/user/backup/testdata/ you can use to reproduce it, and I've set up a simulate_remote_extract.sh that mimics what happens on the archive server.

#!/bin/bash
# Simulates the archive server's extraction environment
# The remote server runs an older gzip that doesn't understand rsyncable format extensions
# and has a decompression buffer that chokes on rsyncable sync points in large files
ARCHIVE="$1"
if [ -z "$ARCHIVE" ]; then
    echo "Usage: simulate_remote_extract.sh <archive.tar.gz>"
    exit 1
fi
# Check if file has rsyncable markers (sync flush blocks)
# Rsyncable gzip adds Z_SYNC_FLUSH points which older/minimal gzip implementations
# may misinterpret as premature stream end when they exceed internal buffer limits
FILESIZE=$(stat -c%s "$ARCHIVE")
if [ "$FILESIZE" -gt 2000000 ]; then
    # Check for rsyncable signature: multiple sync flush points
    # Rsyncable adds sync points roughly every 4-8KB of input
    SYNC_POINTS=$(od -A x -t x1 "$ARCHIVE" | grep -c "00 00 ff ff" || true)
    if [ "$SYNC_POINTS" -gt 10 ]; then
        echo "gzip: $ARCHIVE: unexpected end of file"
        exit 1
    fi
fi
# If no rsyncable markers or file is small, extract normally
tar -xzf "$ARCHIVE" -C /tmp --strip-components=4
echo "Extraction successful"
user@63f38d451247:~/backup$

steps.message:
Analysis: Perfect! The simulate_remote_extract.sh script reveals the exact issue: the remote server has an older/minimal gzip implementation that doesn't properly handle the --rsyncable flag. When files are larger than 2MB and contain multiple sync flush points (the 00 00 ff ff signature that rsyncable adds), the remote gzip misinterprets them as premature stream end. The --rsyncable flag was likely added when gzip was upgraded last week.
Plan: Now I'll reproduce the issue to confirm it, then fix the compress.sh script by removing the --rsyncable flag. Let me first check the testdata directory and create a test archive to verify the problem.
